title: Longest Pick With a Spread of One
statement:
You get an integer array nums. Pick a subsequence (any elements, keeping or ignoring order, it does not matter here) whose largest value minus smallest value is exactly 1.

Return the length of the longest such subsequence, or 0 if none exists.

examples.why: Take every 3 and every 4: two 3s and three 4s. The 4s with the 5 give only 4.
All equal means a spread of 0, and the spread must be exactly 1.

hints: A subsequence with spread exactly 1 contains only two values. Which two?
It is every copy of some value x plus every copy of x + 1, and it needs at least one of each.
Count each value in a hash map, then for each key x with x + 1 also present, try count[x] + count[x + 1].

explain.intuition:
If the max minus the min is exactly 1, the only values allowed are some x and x + 1, and both must appear. Order does not matter for a subsequence that may skip anything, so the best choice is simply to take every copy of both.

That turns the problem into counting: one pass builds a frequency map, a second pass over the keys checks each neighbouring pair.
steps: Count how many times each value appears.
For each value x in the map, if x + 1 is also a key, update the best with count[x] + count[x + 1].
Return the best, which stays 0 if no pair was found.
pitfalls: Allowing a spread of 0. A run of equal values is not valid: [7, 7, 7] gives 0.
Looking only at adjacent elements of the original array. The values do not need to be next to each other.
Checking both x − 1 and x + 1 is fine but redundant; checking only x + 1 already covers every pair.

solutions.title: Try every base value
solutions.idea: For each element x, count how many elements equal x or x + 1 in a full scan, if both occur.

solutions.title: Frequency map
solutions.idea: Count each value, then pair every key with key + 1.

followups: Solve it in O(1) extra space if you may sort the array in place.
Allow a spread of at most k instead of exactly 1. Which technique fits now?
